title: Operating Systems
tagline: Kernel structure, processes and scheduling, address spaces and paging, threads and locks, synchronisation and deadlock, storage, file systems and virtual machines
summary: The operating system turns one machine into many: it shares the processor, memory and devices between programs while protecting them from one another. This course explains how, following the three themes of virtualisation, concurrency and persistence — processes and scheduling, address spaces and paging, threads, locks and deadlock, storage devices and file systems — and ends with virtual machines and containers.
overview: An operating system turns one machine into many. It shares the processor, memory and devices between programs that do not trust one another, gives each of them a simpler and larger machine than the real one — a processor of its own, a private address space, named and persistent files — and protects them, and itself, from each other. This course explains how, from the hardware mechanisms that make protection possible (kernel mode, the timer interrupt, the memory-management unit) to the policies built on them.

The course follows the three themes made standard by the Arpaci-Dusseaus' *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*. **Virtualisation**: the kernel's structure and system calls, processes and CPU scheduling, address translation and paging, and page replacement. **Concurrency**: threads, race conditions and locks built from atomic instructions, then condition variables, semaphores and deadlock. **Persistence**: devices, hard disks, SSDs and RAID, and file systems with their on-disk layout and crash consistency. A final chapter virtualises whole machines and builds containers. The chapters assume [[computer-systems]], whose chapters on exceptions and processes, the memory hierarchy, dynamic memory and system-level I/O are used throughout and not repeated.

Operating systems are hard because they are concurrent, asynchronous and must never fail: an interrupt can arrive between any two instructions, a crash can interrupt any sequence of disk writes, and a bug in the kernel takes down everything above it. The way to learn them is to combine precise models with experiment. Every lesson proves its central results — the optimality of shortest-job-first and of Bélády's algorithm, Peterson's algorithm, the deadlock conditions, the atomicity of journalling, the Popek–Goldberg theorem — and every lesson measures real behaviour on a Linux machine: the cost of a system call and a context switch, the TLB's reach, page faults under copy-on-write, lost updates in a racy program, a deadlock caught by `timeout`, an ext4 file system inspected with `debugfs`, a process confined by namespaces and cgroups. Run the programs, change them, and break them on purpose.
outcomes: Explain how dual-mode operation, the timer interrupt and the MMU let a kernel protect itself and other programs, and why each is necessary.

Trace and compare scheduling policies — FCFS, SJF, SRTF, round robin, MLFQ and weighted fair sharing — computing turnaround, waiting and response times, and prove the optimality of shortest-job-first.
Translate virtual addresses through base-and-bounds, segment and multi-level page tables, and calculate page-table sizes and effective access times with a TLB.
Simulate FIFO, LRU, clock and optimal page replacement, explain Bélády's anomaly and the stack property, and recognise and remedy thrashing.
Identify race conditions in multithreaded code, prove properties of mutual-exclusion algorithms, and implement locks from atomic instructions and futexes.
Solve synchronisation problems with condition variables and semaphores, and prevent, avoid or detect deadlock using lock ordering, the banker's algorithm and resource-allocation graphs.
Analyse the performance of hard disks, SSDs and RAID arrays, including disk scheduling, write amplification and the reliability of redundant arrays.
Describe how file systems lay out inodes, directories and data on disk, and explain how journalling and copy-on-write keep them consistent across crashes.
Explain how hypervisors virtualise the processor, memory and devices, and how containers use namespaces and control groups, and compare the isolation they provide.

chapters.title: Operating-system structure
chapters.summary: Kernel and user mode, system calls, kernel architectures and how the system boots.

chapters.title: Processes and CPU scheduling
chapters.summary: The process abstraction, context switches, and scheduling policies from first-come first-served to multilevel feedback queues.

chapters.title: Address spaces and paging
chapters.summary: Address translation, segmentation, page tables and translation lookaside buffers.

chapters.title: Swapping and page replacement
chapters.summary: Demand paging and page faults, replacement policies such as LRU and the clock algorithm, and thrashing.

chapters.title: Threads and locks
chapters.summary: Threads, race conditions and mutual exclusion, and building locks from atomic instructions.

chapters.title: Condition variables, semaphores and deadlock
chapters.summary: Condition variables, semaphores and monitors, classic synchronisation problems, and preventing and detecting deadlock.

chapters.title: Storage devices and input/output
chapters.summary: Device interaction and drivers, hard disks and solid-state drives, disk scheduling and RAID.

chapters.title: File systems
chapters.summary: Files and directories, on-disk layout and inodes, crash consistency and journalling.

chapters.title: Virtual machines and containers
chapters.summary: Hypervisors, hardware-assisted virtualisation, containers and isolation.

history.title: CTSS demonstrated
history.detail: Fernando Corbató's group at MIT demonstrated the Compatible Time-Sharing System on a modified IBM 709 in November 1961 and described it in a 1962 paper: interactive time sharing with time slicing and a multilevel feedback queue.

history.title: Atlas: paged virtual memory
history.detail: Tom Kilburn and colleagues at Manchester described the Atlas computer's 'one-level storage system', the first paged virtual memory, with demand paging between core and drum.

history.title: Multics and cooperating sequential processes
history.detail: A set of papers at the 1965 Fall Joint Computer Conference described Multics, with hierarchical files and protection rings; in the same year Edsger Dijkstra solved mutual exclusion for n processes and introduced semaphores in 'Cooperating sequential processes'.

history.title: Bélády's study of replacement algorithms
history.detail: László Bélády's IBM Systems Journal paper compared page-replacement algorithms on real traces and introduced the optimal algorithm MIN.

history.title: THE multiprogramming system and the working set
history.detail: Dijkstra's paper on the THE system showed a layered operating system organised with semaphores; Peter Denning introduced the working-set model, explaining thrashing.

history.title: System deadlocks
history.detail: Edward Coffman, Melanie Elphick and Arie Shoshani's survey stated the four necessary conditions for deadlock and the strategies of prevention, avoidance and detection.

history.title: Unix and the Popek–Goldberg theorem
history.detail: Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson's 'The UNIX time-sharing system' appeared in Communications of the ACM; in the same journal and year, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg gave the formal requirements for virtualisable architectures, and Leslie Lamport published the bakery algorithm.

history.title: Peterson's algorithm
history.detail: Gary Peterson published a simple two-process mutual-exclusion algorithm using only reads and writes, still the standard example for proofs of mutual exclusion.

history.title: The Fast File System
history.detail: Marshall McKusick, William Joy, Samuel Leffler and Robert Fabry's FFS introduced cylinder groups and locality-aware allocation, improving Unix file-system throughput up to tenfold.

history.title: Hardware-assisted virtualisation
history.detail: Intel shipped VT-x in 2005 (AMD-V followed in 2006), making the x86 satisfy the Popek–Goldberg condition through a new root/non-root mode; Linux's KVM, built on it, was merged in 2007.

references.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
references.authors: Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau
references.note: Version 1.10, freely available online. The organising text for this course — virtualisation, concurrency, persistence — with clear explanations, simulators and projects; excellent on scheduling, paging, locks and crash consistency.

references.title: Operating System Concepts
references.authors: Abraham Silberschatz, Peter Baer Galvin and Greg Gagne
references.note: Tenth edition. The broadest standard textbook, with careful treatments of scheduling, synchronisation problems, deadlock and the banker's algorithm, and case studies of Linux and Windows.

references.title: Modern Operating Systems
references.authors: Andrew S. Tanenbaum and Herbert Bos
references.note: Fifth edition. Strong on kernel structure, microkernels, virtualisation and security, with detailed Linux, Android and Windows case studies.

references.title: Operating Systems: Principles and Practice
references.note: Second edition, in four volumes. Rigorous and practical on concurrency, with a strong treatment of synchronisation patterns, file systems and reliability.

references.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
references.authors: Randal E. Bryant and David R. O'Hallaron
references.note: Third edition. The prerequisite material from the programmer's side — exceptions, processes, virtual memory, system-level I/O — on which this course builds.

references.title: The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System
references.authors: Marshall Kirk McKusick, George V. Neville-Neil and Robert N. M. Watson
references.note: Second edition. How a real Unix kernel implements processes, virtual memory, file systems (UFS and ZFS) and I/O, by the designers of the Fast File System.
